medium.titulo: Risk-Based Test Selection for Large Playwright Projects: How to Run the Most Important Tests First
medium.resumo: Imagine working on an e-commerce application with 2,000 automated Playwright tests.
medium.conteudo_html:
Imagine working on an e-commerce application with 2,000 automated Playwright tests.

Every time a developer changes one small feature, your automation team runs all 2,000 tests.

The test execution takes several hours.

Developers wait for results. Pull requests remain pending. Small code changes take longer to reach production.

Is running every test the best solution?

Not always.

A better approach is to identify which tests are most important, understand which application areas are affected by code changes, and execute high-risk tests first.

This approach is called Risk-Based Test Selection.

Risk-based test selection helps automation engineers prioritize important test cases based on business impact, application changes, failure probability, and user experience.

In this guide, you will learn how to implement risk-based test selection in large Playwright projects using practical examples, test tagging, Playwright configuration, and CI/CD workflows.

What Is Risk-Based Test Selection?

Risk-based test selection is a software testing approach that identifies and prioritizes test cases according to the risk of application failure.

In simple words, it means:

Instead of running every test with the same priority, run the tests that protect the most important application features first.

For example, consider an online shopping application.

It contains:

  • Login functionality
  • Product search
  • Shopping cart
  • Payment processing
  • Order management
  • User profile
  • Product reviews
  • Wishlist

Are all these features equally important?

No.

If the payment system stops working, customers cannot complete purchases.

If the wishlist page has a minor display problem, customers may still purchase products.

Both issues matter, but their business impact is different.

Therefore, payment testing should receive higher priority than a minor wishlist display test.

The main objective of risk-based test selection is to reduce testing delays without ignoring important application risks.

Why Do Large Playwright Projects Need Risk-Based Test Selection?

A small Playwright project may contain only 20 or 30 test cases.

Running all tests is usually manageable.

However, enterprise applications can contain hundreds or thousands of automated test cases.

As the application grows, several problems appear.

1. Long Test Execution Time

Suppose your Playwright framework contains 1,500 tests.

Running the complete regression suite after every small code change can consume significant CI resources.

Developers may wait longer for feedback.

Risk-based selection helps execute the most important tests earlier.

2. Important Failures May Be Detected Late

Imagine a developer changes the payment calculation logic.

The payment validation test is located near the end of a large regression suite.

If the test suite takes two hours, the team may discover the payment problem much later.

A better approach is to prioritize payment-related tests.

3. Increased CI/CD Costs

Running unnecessary browser tests repeatedly consumes:

  • CI runner time
  • Browser execution resources
  • Infrastructure capacity
  • Storage for reports and traces

Selecting relevant tests can reduce unnecessary execution.

4. Difficulty Managing Large Test Suites

As new features are introduced, test cases increase.

Without proper categorization, automation engineers may struggle to understand:

  • Which tests are critical?
  • Which tests cover payment functionality?
  • Which tests should run before deployment?
  • Which tests can run during nightly regression?

Risk-based selection creates a more organized testing strategy.

How Does Risk-Based Test Selection Work?

A practical risk-based testing process follows six steps.

Step 1: Understand the Application

First, identify the important application modules.

For an e-commerce application:

Application Module

Business Importance

Login

High

Payment

Critical

Checkout

Critical

Product Search

High

Shopping Cart

High

Wishlist

Medium

Product Reviews

Low to Medium

These priorities are examples. Actual business importance depends on the application.

Step 2: Understand the Code Changes

Before selecting tests, understand what changed in the application.

For example:

A developer modifies the payment service.

Ask these questions:

  • Was the payment calculation changed?
  • Was the checkout page modified?
  • Was the payment API updated?
  • Does the change affect order creation?
  • Could existing login or cart functionality be affected?

This helps identify related test cases.

Step 3: Identify Failure Probability

Some application areas have a higher chance of failure after a particular code change.

For example:

If the developer modifies payment calculation logic, payment validation tests become important.

If the developer changes the login authentication service, login and session-related tests become important.

Consider both the possibility of failure and the damage it could cause.

Step 4: Calculate Risk Priority

You can use a simple risk scoring model.

Risk Score = Impact Score × Failure Probability Score

Use a scale from 1 to 5.

Score

Meaning

  1. Very Low

2. Low

3. Medium

4. High

5. Very High

Example:

Test Scenario

Impact

Failure Probability

Risk Score

Payment Processing

5

5

25

Login Validation

5

4

20

Checkout

5

4

20

Product Search

3

3

9

Wishlist Display

2

2

4

Higher scores indicate tests that deserve greater attention.

This is a prioritization aid, not a universal industry formula. Teams should adjust the model according to their application and actual production data.

Step 5: Select the Right Tests

After calculating risk, organize tests into groups.

Critical Tests

Tests protecting payment, authentication, checkout, and other business-critical workflows.

High-Priority Tests

Tests covering important features such as product search, shopping cart, and order management.

Medium-Priority Tests

Tests covering normal application functionality.

Low-Priority Tests

Tests covering minor visual changes or less frequently used functionality.

Step 6: Execute Tests and Analyze Results

Run the selected tests first.

Review:

  • Passed tests
  • Failed tests
  • Execution time
  • Application changes
  • Uncovered functionality

Update the selection when the application changes.

Risk-based test selection should be a continuous process, not a one-time activity.

How to Implement Risk-Based Test Selection in Playwright

Playwright provides test tagging and filtering capabilities that help organize and execute selected test cases.

Let’s understand this using a practical e-commerce example.

Step 1: Organize Playwright Tests Using Tags

Create meaningful test tags based on business importance.

For example:

import { test, expect } from ‘@playwright/test’;

test(‘Payment should complete successfully’,

{ tag: [‘@critical’, ‘@payment’] },

async ({ page }) => {

await page.goto(‘/checkout’);

await page.getByRole(‘button’, {

name: ‘Pay Now’

}).click();

await expect(

page.getByText(‘Payment Successful’)

).toBeVisible();

});

Here:

  • @critical identifies a business-critical test.
  • @payment identifies the application module.
  • The test verifies an important payment workflow.

Tags make it easier to organize large test suites.

Step 2: Create High-Priority Test Cases

Consider a login scenario.

import { test, expect } from ‘@playwright/test’;

test(‘User should log in successfully’,

{ tag: [‘@critical’, ‘@authentication’] },

async ({ page }) => {

await page.goto(‘/login’);

await page.getByLabel(‘Email’)

.fill(‘user@example.com’);

await page.getByLabel(‘Password’)

.fill(process.env.TEST_PASSWORD || ‘’);

await page.getByRole(‘button’, {

name: ‘Login’

}).click();

await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/);

});

This test checks whether a user can successfully access the application.

In a real project, use securely managed test credentials and isolated test accounts.

Step 3: Run Only Critical Tests

You can use Playwright’s — grep option to execute tests matching a tag.

Command:

npx playwright test — grep “@critical”

This command selects tests whose titles or associated tags match @critical.

To execute payment-related tests:

npx playwright test — grep “@payment”

To execute authentication tests:

npx playwright test — grep “@authentication”

This allows automation engineers to execute selected groups without running the entire suite.

Step 4: Run the Complete Regression Suite

Risk-based selection should not permanently replace full regression testing.

For complete regression execution:

npx playwright test

A practical strategy is to execute critical tests during fast feedback stages and schedule broader regression testing at appropriate checkpoints.

Practical Example: Selecting Tests After a Payment Code Change

Imagine your developer modifies the payment API.

Your application contains the following tests:

Test Case

Priority

Execute First?

Successful Payment

Critical

Yes

Failed Payment

Critical

Yes

Duplicate Payment Prevention

Critical

Yes

Order Creation

High

Yes

Shopping Cart Display

Medium

Depends on dependencies

Wishlist Display

Low

Usually not immediately

The team identifies payment-related functionality and executes the most relevant tests first.

However, do not select tests using tags alone.

A payment change might also affect order creation, inventory updates, or transaction history.

The team should examine dependencies and application architecture before finalizing the selection.

This is what makes risk-based testing useful in real enterprise projects.

How to Integrate Risk-Based Test Selection Into CI/CD

A large Playwright framework should have different execution stages.

A practical workflow looks like this:

Developer creates a code change

↓

Pull request is created

↓

Identify changed application modules

↓

Select relevant critical tests

↓

Execute selected Playwright tests

↓

Analyze test results

↓

Run broader regression tests at the appropriate stage

↓

Approve deployment when release criteria are satisfied

For example:

Pipeline Stage

Test Selection

Pull Request

Critical and change-related tests

Main Branch

Broader regression tests

Pre-Production

Release-critical validation

Nightly Execution

Complete regression suite

Production Monitoring

Health and availability checks

This is a suggested architecture. The exact stages should depend on the application’s release process.

Common Mistakes in Risk-Based Test Selection

Mistake 1: Selecting Tests Only by Execution Time

A fast test is not automatically an important test.

A payment validation test may take longer than a simple UI test, but its business value can be much higher.

Prioritize risk and business impact, not just speed.

Mistake 2: Ignoring Application Dependencies

A developer changes the checkout service.

The team selects only checkout tests.

However, checkout may depend on inventory, payment, and order creation.

Ignoring these dependencies can leave important defects undetected.

Mistake 3: Running Only Critical Tests Forever

Critical tests provide fast feedback.

But they cannot guarantee that every application feature works correctly.

Schedule broader regression testing.

Mistake 4: Never Updating Test Priorities

Business requirements change.

A feature that was previously low priority may become critical.

Review risk scores whenever application functionality or business requirements change.

Mistake 5: Using Retries to Hide Failures

A test that fails and passes after retry should be investigated.

Do not automatically consider it a successful validation without understanding the original failure.

Best Practices for Risk-Based Test Selection in Playwright

  1. Identify business-critical application workflows.
  2. Maintain clear test tags.
  3. Map tests to application modules.
  4. Understand code changes before selecting tests.
  5. Consider application dependencies.
  6. Prioritize tests using business impact and failure probability.
  7. Execute critical tests early in CI/CD.
  8. Run broader regression tests regularly.
  9. Monitor flaky tests and investigate repeated failures.
  10. Update test priorities as the application evolves.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. What is risk-based test selection in Playwright?

Risk-based test selection is a testing approach that prioritizes Playwright test cases according to application risk, business impact, and the probability of failure.

2. How do I select critical tests in a large Playwright project?

Identify important application modules, understand code changes, evaluate business impact, map related test cases, and execute high-priority tests first.

3. Can Playwright execute tests based on tags?

Yes. Playwright supports test tagging and filtering through options such as — grep and — grep-invert.

4. Should I run the complete regression suite after every code change?

Not necessarily. Teams can run relevant tests first and execute broader regression suites at suitable stages. However, test selection must account for dependencies and potential impacts beyond directly changed files.

5. Does risk-based testing replace regression testing?

No. Risk-based testing helps prioritize test execution. Regression testing remains important for identifying defects in existing functionality.

6. Is risk-based testing useful for enterprise applications?

Yes. It is particularly useful for applications with large test suites, complex dependencies, frequent releases, and business-critical workflows.

7. What is the difference between risk-based testing and test prioritization?

Risk-based testing evaluates application risks and uses that information to guide testing decisions. Test prioritization is the process of ordering or selecting test cases based on those decisions.

Final Thoughts

Running thousands of Playwright tests is not always the fastest way to identify important application failures.

The real challenge is understanding which tests matter most, which application areas are affected by code changes, and which failures could create the biggest problems for users.

Risk-based test selection helps automation engineers make better testing decisions.

Start by identifying critical workflows, organizing tests using tags, understanding application dependencies, and integrating selected tests into your CI/CD pipeline.

As your Playwright framework grows, this approach can help your team achieve faster feedback and more controlled releases.

Want to learn how to build and manage enterprise-level Playwright automation frameworks?

Explore practical Playwright automation concepts, CI/CD integration, API testing, framework development, and real-time projects at Playwright Masters.

medium.titulo: AI can now prove your code is safe, not just test it
medium.resumo: Anthropic used an AI to write math proofs for 123 open-source libraries. Here is what that means in plain words, and where it stops.
medium.conteudo_html:
Anthropic used an AI to write math proofs for 123 open-source libraries. Here is what that means in plain words, and where it stops.

Testing tells you the code worked for the inputs you tried.

A proof tells you it works for every input.

That second thing used to be rare. It was slow, expensive, and needed a very small group of experts.

On Oct 22, 2026, Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team, working with a company called Theorem, published research saying that is changing. They used their model, Claude, to write proofs for real open-source code at a scale nobody had done before.

All the numbers below are Anthropic’s, from their post. I have linked it at the end.

First, what is formal verification?

Formal verification means you turn code into a math model.

Then you try to prove it always follows a rule you wrote down.

The rule is called the spec. Spec just means “what correct looks like.”

If the proof works, the rule holds for every input, not only the ones you tested.

If the proof fails, the place where it fails often points right at a bug.

A separate program, called a proof checker, checks the proof line by line. So you do not have to trust whoever wrote the proof. You only have to trust the checker and the rule.

Why almost nobody did it

Proofs are huge. They are often many times bigger than the code itself.

They also need a niche skill set.

Anthropic gives one example. The seL4 operating system kernel took about 2 person-years to build.

Proving it correct took about 20 person-years.

So proofs stayed in places where failure is not an option, like the flight software at Airbus.

What they actually did

They started with fuzz tests.

A fuzz test throws huge numbers of random, mutated inputs at a piece of code and waits for a crash. Any crash is a bug.

Google runs this for many open-source projects through a program called OSS-Fuzz.

The catch is simple. Fuzzing is brute force. It can never try every input.

So they turned each fuzz test into a rule: “this test never crashes, for any input up to 64 MB.”

Then they asked Claude to prove that rule.

Not on the source code. On the compiled machine code for RISC-V, a type of processor design like x86 or ARM.

Here is what came out, over a few weeks:

  • Proofs that 239 test entry points across 123 libraries never crash for inputs up to 64 MB.
  • About 180 million lines of proof in total.
  • A typical proof ran to about 600,000 lines, for programs with a median size of about 18,000 machine instructions.

Nobody reads 600,000 lines. That is the point of the proof checker. It reads them instead.

The bugs it found along the way

Trying to prove “this never crashes” is a great way to find out why it does.

When Claude got stuck, it was often stuck on a real bug. It patched the bug and kept going.

Some examples Anthropic gives:

  • A counter bug in a decompressor that caused an out-of-bounds write. It only showed up on inputs of around 20 MB with one rare layout.
  • An out-of-bounds read in an image decoder. It needed a 64 MB input and over 2 GB of memory.
  • A rediscovery of a known security bug in libexpat, a popular XML parser, that needed deeply nested input.
  • A file restriction feature in one library that was not always enforced. That one never crashed at all. It was just wrong.

Most fuzzers use small inputs, often capped at 1 MB. Bugs that need 20 MB of one exact shape are very hard to stumble into by chance.

Anthropic’s summary line: these bugs survived years of detection “despite trillions of test runs.”

It goes beyond “does not crash”

This part is easy to miss.

Many fuzz tests check a real property and crash on purpose if it breaks.

For example, a compression test can say: compress the input, decompress it, and crash if the result is different.

So a proof that this test never crashes is a proof that compression always round-trips correctly.

They also tried other kinds of proofs:

  • Claude wrote a formal spec of the zlib compression format and proved the Linux kernel’s zlib code follows it.
  • Claude built a Python interpreter in Rust and proved it follows a published description of how Python behaves. Across 1.7 million random Python programs, it matched real Python in 99.95% of them.
  • While trying to verify a widely used PDF reader, they found as many security bugs in one week as are usually reported in a year.

What Anthropic says it does not prove

Their own limits section is worth reading. In short:

“Formally verified” does not mean “bug free.”

The proofs assume a single-threaded program on RISC-V, linked a certain way. Most real users run x86 or ARM with a different setup.

They did not verify every entry point, and entry points do not cover a whole library.

The memory checker they relied on does not catch every memory bug.

A program that calls the library the wrong way can still break things.

Cost is real too. Proofs can take hundreds of millions of tokens. Tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads and writes, and you pay for them.

They are publishing the trusted parts and a subset of the proofs so anyone can check them.

What the critics said

The Hacker News thread passed 470 points and 300 comments. The pushback was sharp and fair.

“Verified against what?” A proof is only as good as the rule you wrote. If the rule is wrong, a perfect proof proves the wrong thing.

“Can the AI cheat?” One developer said that when they use AI with proof tools, it tries to remove the checks instead of passing them. Anthropic admits this risk. They call it reward hacking: the model could make a rule easy to prove by changing the program. They say they penalized patches and audited them.

“The proofs are bloated.” Anthropic’s own appendix says the AI writes very long, repetitive proofs where a human expert would build cleaner building blocks. A commenter quoted it and asked if this style can scale to harder programs.

“Normal teams will not bother.” One commenter expects proofs to stay in already careful fields like cryptography and aerospace, while everyone else ships faster instead.

There was support too.

Several people pointed out that this is strictly stronger than fuzzing. A fuzzer samples inputs. A proof covers all of them, up to the limit.

And one engineer said they already do something like this at work: an AI opens a speed-up change with a proof that it behaves the same as the old code.

Where this fits first

You will not prove your whole app next week.

But some code is small, critical, and has a clear rule:

  • Parsers and decoders that read untrusted files.
  • Compression code.
  • Crypto code.
  • Payment and money math.
  • Shared libraries that thousands of other programs depend on.

That is where “prove it” starts to make sense.

Anthropic also argues proofs can be reused. When agents could copy each other’s finished proofs, they needed 17% fewer tokens. Prove a popular library once, and everything on top of it benefits.

The plain takeaway

Testing asks: did it break on what I tried?

Proving asks: can it ever break, under these rules?

AI just made the second question much cheaper to ask.

It did not make writing the rules any easier. That part is still on us.

Sources

  • Anthropic, “LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale” (Oct 22, 2026): https://www.anthropic.com/research/formal-verification
  • Hacker News discussion: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50202217

medium.titulo: Your Agent’s Context Fills Up Before You Type: What to Trim First
medium.resumo: Most advice about coding agents is about what you type. But by the time you type your first prompt, the agent’s context window is already…
medium.conteudo_html:
Most advice about coding agents is about what you type. But by the time you type your first prompt, the agent’s context window is already partly full: instruction files, memory, tool names, skill descriptions. Then every file it reads, every test run and every long log adds more, and all of it is re-sent with every request.

That matters for more than your bill. In Effective context engineering for AI agents, Anthropic describes context rot: as the number of tokens in the window grows, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from it goes down. Their framing is that a model has an “attention budget”, and every token you add spends some of it. The guiding principle they give is to “find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome.”

I covered the money side in Where Your Coding Agent’s Token Bill Goes. This one is about quality: what fills the context, and what to trim first so the agent has room to think about your actual task. The examples use Claude Code because its docs spell out exactly what loads and when, but the order works for any agent.

Step 1: Look before you cut

Don’t guess. In Claude Code, run /context. The context window docs describe it as a live breakdown by category, with optimization suggestions, including which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files loaded.

According to the same page, this is what loads before you type anything:

  • CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md in its place) and auto memory
  • MCP tool names
  • skill descriptions
  • anything your own setup adds, like an output style or --append-system-prompt text

Write down the three biggest categories. That’s your trim list, in order. If you don’t use Claude Code, the question is the same: what does your agent load at startup, and which of those things did you actually need today?

Step 2: Trim the tools

Anthropic calls bloated tool sets “one of the most common failure modes”: too much functionality, or tools that overlap so the model can’t tell which one to use. Their test is a good one to borrow: if a human engineer can’t say for sure which tool fits a situation, the agent can’t be expected to do better.

Claude Code already softens the cost here. Per its MCP docs, tool search is on by default, so only tool names and server instructions enter context at session start; full definitions load when Claude actually needs a tool. That doesn’t make every connected server free, though, and it doesn’t fix overlapping tools. Three things still help:

  1. Disable servers you aren’t using. Run /mcp and switch off anything unrelated to the current project.
  2. Prefer a CLI when one exists. The cost docs say tools like gh, aws, gcloud and sentry-cli are still more context-efficient than MCP servers, because they don't add any per-tool listing.
  3. Check tool search is actually on. It’s off in some setups, for example older models, some cloud deployments or when ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false is set, and then all MCP tools load upfront. If /context shows a large tools category, this is the first thing to look at.

If you write your own MCP server, the docs suggest keeping descriptions and server instructions concise and putting the important words near the start, since that’s the part tool search reads.

Step 3: Trim what loads from files

Instruction files load every session, whether the task needs them or not. Claude Code’s memory docs recommend keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, and note that imports help you organise a long file but don't reduce its context cost, because imported files load with it.

The fix is to move instructions to where they’re needed:

  • Path-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ load only when Claude works with matching files.
  • Skills load only when invoked, so a long PR-review or migration procedure costs nothing on days you don’t use it.

A path-scoped rule looks like this:

---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API rules
- Every endpoint validates input with the shared schema.
- Errors use the standard error response format.

I went through the full cut-and-move process in Your CLAUDE.md Is Too Long, so I won’t repeat it here. One addition that’s easy to miss is in Step 5 below: path-scoped rules don’t survive compaction the way root instructions do.

Then look at what the agent reads during work. Vague prompts trigger broad scanning; the cost docs contrast “improve this codebase” with “add input validation to the login function in auth.ts”. The second one lets the agent find what it needs with far fewer file reads.

Step 4: Keep noisy output out of the main window

Test runs, log files and documentation pages are the quiet context killers. A failing test suite can print thousands of lines when you needed ten.

Two options from the docs:

  • Filter before the model sees it. The cost docs show a PreToolUse hook that rewrites test commands to keep only failure lines, and give the example of a hook that greps a 10,000-line log for ERROR instead of letting Claude read all of it.
  • Delegate to a subagent. A subagent does the reading in its own context window and sends back only a summary. The docs recommend this for running tests, fetching documentation and processing logs. It isn’t free, since the subagent’s requests still count toward your usage, but the raw output stays out of your main conversation.

Anthropic’s post lists the same idea from the other direction: once a tool result is deep in history, the agent rarely needs to see the raw output again, and clearing old tool results is one of the lightest forms of compaction.

Step 5: Manage history on purpose

The longest-lived thing in your context is the conversation itself. You have two tools for it, and they do different things.

/clear when the task changes. Old conversation crowds out the files you need next and is re-sent with every message. The docs point out that /clear costs nothing, while /compact is itself a large request because it has to read the whole conversation it summarises. If you don't need continuity, clear. Use /rename first if you want to /resume that session later.

/compact with a focus when you do need continuity. Claude Code compacts automatically near the limit, but the automatic pass guesses what matters. Telling it is better:

/compact focus on the auth bug fix

You can also put standing instructions in your project’s CLAUDE.md, as the docs show:

# Compact instructions

When you are using compact, please focus on test output and code changes

Before relying on compaction, know what comes back. Per the context window docs, after compaction:

  • the project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules and auto memory are re-injected from disk;
  • path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files are summarised away and reload only when Claude touches a matching file again;
  • Claude Code re-reads up to five recently modified files it had used, and a file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference, not its content;
  • invoked skill bodies are re-injected but capped, and truncation keeps the start of the file.

So if a rule must hold for the whole session, don’t scope it to paths; put it in the root file. And put the most important instructions at the top of each skill.

If you’re building your own agent rather than using Claude Code, the same three techniques from Anthropic’s post apply: compaction, structured note-taking (the agent writes notes to a file outside the window and reads them back later), and subagents with clean context windows.

A 15-minute context check

  1. Run /context (or your agent's equivalent) and note the three biggest categories.
  2. Disable MCP servers you don’t need for this project.
  3. Replace an MCP server with its CLI where one exists.
  4. Confirm tool search is on if your tools category looks large.
  5. Get each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines; move the rest to path-scoped rules or skills.
  6. Write prompts that name the file or function, not the whole codebase.
  7. Filter test and log output with a hook, or send it to a subagent.
  8. /clear between unrelated tasks; /compact with a focus when you need continuity.
  9. Keep session-wide rules unscoped, at the top of the root instruction file.
  10. Run /context again and compare.

Where to go next

These five steps are one slice of a bigger discipline. Context Engineering: The Complete Guide to the Skill That Replaced Prompt Engineering covers it in 40 pages: the anatomy of a context window, the four core strategies (Write, Select, Compress, Isolate) in depth, the four failure modes (poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash) with a diagnostic toolkit, context engineering in Claude Code and Cursor, 20 reusable patterns, 12 common pitfalls with fixes, and a 30-day plan.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by the author.

Artificial Intelligence continues to influence the global technology industry, and Generative AI is becoming an important part of business operations. From automated customer support to intelligent software development, organizations are exploring new ways to use AI to improve productivity and customer experiences.

In 2026, understanding generative AI applications can provide valuable career opportunities for students, fresh graduates, and working professionals. A Generative AI Course in Telugu offers an accessible way to understand emerging technologies and explore relevant career paths.

Why Is Generative AI Important in 2026?

Generative AI enables computers to produce new content, understand natural language instructions, summarize information, and assist with complex tasks.

Businesses are adopting AI-powered solutions in areas such as:

  • Customer service automation.
  • Software development assistance.
  • Marketing content generation.
  • Business data analysis.
  • Document processing.
  • Personalized learning.
  • Knowledge management.

As organizations explore these applications, professionals with practical AI knowledge can contribute to technology and business projects.

Top Generative AI Career Opportunities in 2026

1. Generative AI Developer

Generative AI Developers create applications using language models, AI APIs, and development frameworks. They build chatbots, content-generation applications, and intelligent assistants.

2. Prompt Engineer

Prompt Engineers design and optimize instructions for AI models to produce relevant and useful responses. Their work may involve testing prompts, improving outputs, and developing reusable prompt templates.

3. AI Application Developer

AI Application Developers integrate artificial intelligence features into websites, mobile applications, and enterprise software. They combine programming knowledge with AI APIs and application development skills.

4. LLM Application Developer

These professionals develop applications powered by Large Language Models. Their work may involve API integration, context management, RAG pipelines, and response evaluation.

5. Machine Learning Engineer

Machine Learning Engineers develop, train, evaluate, and deploy machine learning systems. This role generally requires strong programming, mathematics, statistics, and machine learning knowledge.

6. AI Automation Specialist

AI Automation Specialists explore how generative AI can support repetitive business processes. They develop workflows for document processing, customer communication, reporting, and task automation.

7. AI Solutions Engineer

AI Solutions Engineers help organizations identify business problems and implement suitable AI-based solutions. They may work with technical teams to integrate models into existing systems.

Which Industries Are Using Generative AI?

Generative AI has applications across several business sectors.

Information Technology: Developers use AI assistants for coding support, debugging, documentation, and software development workflows.

Education: AI-powered learning assistants can support personalized explanations, practice questions, and educational content preparation.

Healthcare: Generative AI can assist with administrative documentation, information retrieval, and other supervised workflows. Clinical applications require appropriate professional oversight.

Banking and Finance: Organizations explore AI for customer communication, document summarization, and internal knowledge management.

Digital Marketing: Marketing professionals use AI tools for content ideation, campaign planning, audience research, and creative development.

E-Commerce: AI applications can support product descriptions, customer assistance, and personalized shopping experiences.

Skills Required to Build a Career in Generative AI

To explore these opportunities, learners should develop the following skills:

  • AI Fundamentals: Understand machine learning, deep learning, and neural networks.
  • Prompt Engineering: Learn how to communicate effectively with generative models.
  • Python Programming: Develop coding skills for AI application development.
  • Large Language Models: Understand LLM capabilities and limitations.
  • AI APIs: Learn how to connect applications with external AI models.
  • RAG: Understand document retrieval and knowledge-based AI systems.
  • Communication: Explain technical solutions and collaborate with development teams.
  • Problem-Solving: Identify practical business problems that AI can help address.

How to prepare for Generative AI Jobs in 2026

Start with the fundamentals and gradually move toward advanced concepts. Choose a structured Generative AI Course in Telugu that explains important technologies with practical demonstrations.

Build projects such as AI chatbots, document assistants, automated email generators, and knowledge-based question-answering applications.

Create a professional portfolio with project descriptions, technologies used, GitHub repositories, and demonstrations. Prepare for technical interviews by understanding Python, LLMs, APIs, RAG, and practical implementation.

Remember that completing a course alone does not guarantee employment. Demonstrable skills, consistent practice, and interview preparation are important for career development.

How to Choose the Best Generative AI Course in Telugu

Before selecting a training program, check the curriculum, trainer experience, practical assignments, real-time projects, and learning support.

A comprehensive program should introduce AI fundamentals, prompt engineering, LLM applications, Python, APIs, RAG, and relevant development tools.

Choose training that balances conceptual understanding with hands-on implementation rather than focusing only on demonstrations of AI tools.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

1. What are the best career opportunities in Generative AI in 2026?

Some relevant roles include Generative AI Developer, LLM Application Developer, AI Application Developer, Prompt Engineer, and Machine Learning Engineer.

2. Is Generative AI a good career option for freshers?

It can be a promising career direction for freshers who develop relevant technical skills, complete practical projects, and understand industry requirements.

3. Can non-IT students learn Generative AI?

Yes. Non-IT students can begin with AI fundamentals, commonly used AI applications, and prompt engineering before progressing toward programming and development.

4. What programming language is useful for Generative AI?

Python is one of the most widely used programming languages for AI development, machine learning, and LLM-based applications.

5. What should I learn before applying for Generative AI jobs?

Focus on Python, AI fundamentals, prompt engineering, LLMs, APIs, RAG, project development, and technical interview preparation.

Conclusion

Generative AI is creating opportunities across technology, education, finance, healthcare, marketing, and other industries. Developing practical knowledge can help learners explore these emerging career paths. Enrolling in a structured Generative AI Course in Telugu, building real-time projects, and continuously improving technical skills can provide a strong foundation for pursuing AI-related opportunities in 2026.

medium.titulo: Using Customer Feedback to Prioritize Design System Improvements
medium.resumo: Build a design system roadmap from customer needs, support evidence, accessibility findings, and adoption friction with clear priorities…
medium.conteudo_html:
Build a design system roadmap from customer needs, support evidence, accessibility findings, and adoption friction with clear priorities and measurable outcomes.

Customer feedback helps a design system team discover where shared components and patterns are failing in real products. A request for another table option may reveal a difficult reporting task. Repeated questions about a form component may point to missing guidance, an unsuitable API, or an accessibility barrier. The first step is to understand the problem behind the requested change.

Effective design system prioritization connects that problem to evidence, affected users, implementation cost, and an observable outcome. A clear process lets teams decide which improvements belong in the shared system, which need product-specific work, and which require more research before engineering begins.

Collect feedback from customers and consuming teams

A design system has at least two important audiences: the designers and engineers who build with it, and the people who use the resulting products. Developer feedback explains integration friction; customer research explains whether the completed experience works. Review both before concluding that a component request represents a broader need.

  • Support reports: identify blocked tasks, confusing messages, recurring workarounds, and recovery failures.
  • Usability research: observe how people understand and operate patterns in a complete journey.
  • Accessibility evaluations: identify keyboard, focus, naming, contrast, and assistive technology barriers.
  • Integration issues: collect component versions, framework details, reproducible examples, and unexpected API behavior.
  • Adoption reviews: investigate local forks, duplicate components, abandoned migrations, and missing documentation.

Give these channels one shared tracking process without requiring everyone to use the same reporting tool. A support team can submit a structured summary on behalf of a customer. Keep sensitive account details and research recordings in access-controlled systems, and use sanitized descriptions in broadly visible planning records.

Use a feedback intake template that captures the problem

Ask for enough detail to investigate, while keeping the reporting effort manageable. Reproduction steps are especially useful for defects; proposed enhancements need the task, current limitation, and evidence of repeated need. Do not make a fully developed solution a prerequisite for reporting a barrier.

Component or pattern: Data table
Installed version: Record the affected release
Affected task: Review selected invoices across multiple pages
Observed problem: Selection state is unclear after pagination
Expected outcome: Users can identify and review selected invoices
Evidence:
- Minimal reproduction or sanitized recording
- Browser, input method, and relevant environment
- Independent teams or products reporting the same behavior
- Research observations, where available
Current workaround: Separate application-level selection summary
Impact: Additional implementation work and user confusion
Owner: Design system triage team
Next action: Reproduce and classify the underlying issue

Separate observed facts from interpretations. “Three teams implemented separate selection summaries” is evidence. “Every customer needs a new table component” is a conclusion that still needs validation. Record uncertainty explicitly so the roadmap does not turn an early assumption into an engineering commitment.

Group related reports without losing important context

Create a problem record for a repeated theme and associate individual reports with it. Preserve differences in component version, device, task, and integration. Similar symptoms can have different causes: one focus failure may originate in a shared dialog, while another comes from how an application opens it.

Count independent affected teams and known usage contexts rather than raw message volume. Ten follow-up comments on one ticket are not ten separate customers. At the same time, low reporting volume does not establish low impact. A barrier that prevents a smaller group from completing a critical task can deserve immediate action.

Review the problem record with product teams before choosing a shared solution. The best intervention might be a documentation example, an integration fix, a component patch, a new pattern, or a product-specific change. Expanding a public API should follow a demonstrated need and a maintenance plan.

Build a design system prioritization rubric

Begin with severity triage. Critical task blockers and serious regressions need an explicit response path rather than waiting for a weighted backlog score. Then compare planned improvements using a consistent rubric. The following dimensions are a practical starting point that a team can adapt to its own product portfolio.

  • User impact: whether the issue blocks completion, creates errors, slows a task, or causes minor friction.
  • Reach: independently affected products, teams, and usage contexts, with unknown reach clearly marked.
  • Evidence confidence: reproducible defects and observed research findings versus an untested request.
  • Workaround cost: repeated application code, support burden, maintenance, and the quality of available alternatives.
  • Strategic fit: connection to agreed product goals, supported patterns, and current platform commitments.
  • Total effort: research, implementation, testing, documentation, migration, and ongoing support.

If the team uses scores, publish definitions for each level and keep the rationale beside the result. Avoid presenting a rough estimate as a precise prediction. Two similarly ranked items may need a small discovery task to reduce uncertainty before either enters delivery. Review dependencies and available capacity alongside the score.

Shared value also matters when deciding whether to add a component. The GOV.UK Design System contribution criteria ask for evidence of usefulness across teams and consider whether a proposal duplicates existing patterns. These are useful questions for evaluating whether a customer request belongs in a reusable system.

Example: prioritize a table improvement over a cosmetic variant

Consider two hypothetical requests. One asks for an additional decorative badge style used by a single product. The other reports that users cannot reliably understand which invoices remain selected when changing table pages. Several consuming teams have implemented their own selection summaries.

Investigate the table behavior first if evidence confirms that it disrupts an important task. Reproduce it in the shared component and in an application to establish ownership. Determine whether the missing behavior belongs to the table primitive or to a higher-level selection pattern. This avoids adding unrelated responsibilities to the core API.

Define acceptance criteria before implementation

  • Selection persistence follows an explicit rule across pagination and filtering.
  • Users can identify selected items and review or clear them using supported input methods.
  • Bulk actions explain which items they affect and provide appropriate recovery or confirmation.
  • Loading, empty, partial-selection, and error states have documented behavior.
  • Consuming teams can adopt the change with clear compatibility and migration guidance.

The badge request can still receive a useful response. An existing token or composition pattern might satisfy it, or the request may remain under consideration until broader need appears. Explain that decision and what new evidence would change it.

Publish a roadmap with decisions and next steps

Give each feedback item a meaningful status such as received, investigating, planned, in progress, released, or declined. Distinguish “needs evidence” from “will not pursue” so reporters understand whether they can help move the discussion forward. Assign an owner and a next review point for active investigations.

A Now, Next, and Later roadmap can communicate direction without implying a delivery date for every idea. Include the problem being addressed, intended outcome, dependencies, and reason for priority. Keep confidential customer evidence separate from the explanation shared with the wider community.

Set an acknowledgement target the team can maintain and explain how urgent barriers should be raised. Acknowledgement confirms that a report is being reviewed; it should not be confused with a promise to deliver a fix within the same period.

Include component quality and migration in the delivery plan

Validate proposed behavior with consuming teams before finalizing the API. Create examples for the states reported in feedback, then review keyboard operation, accessible names, responsive content, and integration boundaries. Add automated regression checks where they can verify the behavior, together with manual assessment for qualities they cannot prove.

Account for design assets, documentation, release notes, and consumer upgrades as part of the work. A breaking change needs explicit migration instructions and a realistic transition plan. If the system supports several framework packages, track parity and compatibility rather than assuming a fix in one implementation reaches all consumers.

Close the feedback loop after release

Tell reporters which release contains the improvement, what changed, and what they need to do to adopt it. Ask affected teams to verify the result in their real workflow. Mark the implementation as released while tracking adoption separately; a merged pull request does not establish that the customer’s barrier has been removed.

Feedback becomes valuable when a reported problem leads to an explainable decision and a verified outcome.

For declined or deferred items, provide the reasoning and a supported alternative where one exists. Review unresolved themes periodically because new adoption evidence or product changes can alter the decision. Keep the history available so new team members do not have to reconstruct the same discussion.

Measure whether design system improvements reach users

Combine process measures with outcome measures. Fast acknowledgement is useful, but it cannot show whether the system became easier to use. Establish a baseline for each major improvement and identify when the team will review the result.

  • Triage health: time to acknowledgement, time to a decision, and age of unresolved high-impact reports.
  • Adoption: affected applications using the corrected component or recommended pattern.
  • Repeated work: reduction in local workarounds and duplicated implementation effort.
  • Quality: recurrence of the original defect, new regressions, and verified accessibility barriers.
  • User outcomes: observed task completion, recovery difficulties, and support contacts related to the reported problem.

Interpret trends within their context. Fewer reports might mean improvement, lower usage, or difficulty finding the reporting channel. Compare equivalent periods and review qualitative evidence alongside counts. Avoid ranking individual teams by ticket volume, since active reporting can indicate healthy participation.

Start with a small, repeatable feedback review

Choose one recurring component problem, gather its independent reports, and confirm the underlying need. Apply the rubric, publish the decision, and define the smallest useful improvement. Reserve capacity for validation and consumer adoption as well as implementation.

After release, review the evidence with reporters and update the backlog accordingly. Repeating this cycle gives the roadmap a clear connection to customer needs while keeping the design system coherent, maintainable, and useful across products.

medium.titulo: Nuxt 前端框架，還有 Server Middleware？從 HTTP 安全標頭開始和 nosniff
medium.resumo: 使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫
medium.conteudo_html:
使用 Vue 開發時，我認為前端負責畫面，後端負責 API 和資料庫

最近在處理 Nuxt 網站的安全性設定時

Nuxt 明明是前端框架

卻可以透過 server/middleware 修改伺服器回傳的 HTTP Header？

原來 Nuxt 不只是 Vue 的前端開發工具，它也具備伺服器端的執行能力

Nuxt 不只是前端框架

在一般 Vue SPA（Single Page Application）中

伺服器主要提供 HTML、CSS 和 JavaScript 檔案

瀏覽器下載後，再由 JavaScript 產生畫面

Nuxt 則支援 SSR（Server-Side Rendering，伺服器端渲染）。

// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  ssr: true
})

當 SSR 啟用時

Nuxt 可以先在伺服器執行 Vue 程式、產生 HTML，再傳送給瀏覽器。

瀏覽器收到 HTML 後，會再透過 JavaScript 接手互動功能

這個過程稱為 Hydration。

因此 Nuxt 的程式可能在兩個不同環境執行：

  • Server（伺服器）：產生 HTML、處理 HTTP 請求。
  • Client（瀏覽器）：呈現畫面、處理使用者互動。

Nuxt 使用的伺服器引擎叫做 Nitro

它可以處理 SSR、Server API 和 Server Middleware。

Middleware 是什麼？

Middleware 中文稱為「中介軟體」。

可以把它想成辦公大樓的警衛。

當有人準備進入辦公室時，警衛會先檢查身分，確認符合條件才讓他進去。

Middleware 也是類似的概念

在主要處理流程之前，先執行某些工作。

Nuxt 有兩種容易搞混的 Middleware。

Route Middleware

放在：middleware/

主要處理頁面導航

例如檢查使用者是否登入。

export default defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to) => {
  const isLoggedIn = false

  if (!isLoggedIn && to.path !== '/login') {
    return navigateTo('/login')
  }
})

Server Middleware

放在：server/middleware/

主要處理進入 Nitro 的 HTTP 請求

例如記錄請求資訊、設定 HTTP Response Header。

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(event, 'X-Content-Type-Options', 'nosniff')
})

兩者最大的差別是：

  • Route Middleware：處理使用者要前往哪個頁面。
  • Server Middleware：處理伺服器收到的 HTTP 請求。

為什麼需要 X-Content-Type-Options？

當瀏覽器向伺服器索取檔案時

伺服器會透過 Content-Type 告訴瀏覽器檔案類型。

Content-Type: text/html
Content-Type: application/javascript
Content-Type: text/css

但某些情況下，瀏覽器可能根據檔案內容自行猜測類型。

這種行為稱為 MIME Sniffing。

伺服器回傳：

Content-Type: text/plain

但檔案內容卻是：

alert("Hello!")

伺服器宣告這是普通文字，但內容看起來像 JavaScript。

如果瀏覽器在載入腳本時自行猜測類型並執行，就可能增加安全風險。

因此可以設定：

X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

要求瀏覽器在載入 JavaScript、CSS 等資源時，遵守對應的 MIME 類型檢查。

如果宣告的類型不符合要求，瀏覽器就會阻擋載入，而不是自行猜測後繼續使用。

使用 Server Middleware 設定安全標頭

在 Nuxt 專案建立：

server/middleware/security-headers.ts

import {
  defineEventHandler,
  setResponseHeader
} from 'h3'

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  setResponseHeader(
    event,
    'X-Content-Type-Options',
    'nosniff'
  )
})

這段程式其實只做一件事情：

在 Nuxt 伺服器處理 HTTP 請求時，替回應加入 X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff。

逐行來看：

  • defineEventHandler()：建立一個 HTTP 請求處理函式。
  • event：代表這次 HTTP 請求與回應的相關資訊。
  • setResponseHeader()：替 HTTP 回應設定 Header。
  • X-Content-Type-Options：安全標頭名稱。
  • nosniff：要求瀏覽器遵守對應資源的 MIME 類型限制。

因為檔案放在 server/middleware/，Nuxt 會自動註冊這段程式。

不需要在每個 Vue 頁面重複設定。

不過要注意，這個 Middleware 只能影響經過 Nitro 處理的 HTTP 回應。

如果正式環境還有 IIS、Nginx 或其他 Web Server 直接提供檔案，就需要另外確認。

如何驗證設定成功？

啟動 Nuxt 專案後，可以使用 Chrome 開發者工具確認。

  1. 按下 F12 開啟 DevTools。
  2. 選擇 Network。
  3. 重新整理網頁。
  4. 點選網頁的 Document 請求。
  5. 查看 Response Headers。
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html;charset=utf-8
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

這代表目前檢查的 HTTP 回應已經包含安全標頭。

另外，也應檢查 JavaScript 和 CSS 是否具有正確的 Content-Type

避免新增 nosniff 後造成檔案載入失敗。

重點整理

  • Nuxt 不只是前端工具，也具備透過 Nitro 執行伺服器端程式的能力。
  • SSR 可以在伺服器先產生 HTML，再交由瀏覽器接手互動。
  • Route Middleware 負責頁面導航與路由檢查。

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Entenda por que a influenciadora Thalya Hill deveria ter sido desclassificada em Belém. Veja também a morte rara por rabdomiólise em Nova York, o banimento vitalício em Dublin e a parceria entre Vega Sports e Sympla. E mais: cupons para Fla Run, Mountain Do e Uphill Corcovado.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 4 de novembro de 2026

A influenciadora Thalya Hill, que foi campeã geral em uma etapa do Circuito Desbrava em Belém (PA), deveria ter sido desclassificada. Embora a polêmica nas redes tenha se concentrado no fato de o campeão masculino ter esperado por ela para cruzarem a linha de chegada juntos, a real infração foi outra: o uso incorreto do número de peito. Durante a prova, a atleta correu com o número preso no short, na altura da coxa. De acordo com as regras da World Athletics e da Confederação Brasileira de Atletismo (CBAt), o número de peito deve ser usado de forma visível na parte da frente do tronco, que é a região que vai da virilha ao pescoço. O descumprimento dessa regra em uma competição oficial é motivo para desclassificação. A medida serve para facilitar a identificação dos atletas pelos árbitros e pela cronometragem.

Fla Run 2026 no Aterro do Flamengo

A segunda etapa da Fla Run, a corrida oficial do Flamengo, já tem data marcada: 29 de novembro de 2026. O evento acontecerá no Aterro do Flamengo, no Rio de Janeiro, com percursos de 3 km, 5 km e 10 km. Para quem quiser participar, as inscrições já estão abertas e é possível garantir 10% de desconto usando o cupom CORRIDANOAR10. Eu posso ser corintiano, mas no Rio de Janeiro meu time é o Flamengo! O link para se inscrever está disponível aqui.

Corredora de 24 anos morre por rabdomiólise na Maratona de Nova York

Uma notícia triste marcou a Maratona de Nova York. A corredora americana Rachel Apa, de apenas 24 anos, faleceu após passar mal a cerca de 3 km da linha de chegada. Ela teve um mal súbito, foi levada ao hospital e a causa da morte foi atribuída à rabdomiólise, uma condição rara em maratonas. A rabdomiólise é uma lesão muscular grave e generalizada, causada por esforço físico extenuante. A destruição das fibras musculares libera substâncias tóxicas na corrente sanguínea, que podem levar à insuficiência renal e, em casos extremos, a uma parada cardíaca. Os principais sintomas de alerta são dor muscular muito intensa, fraqueza e urina escura, com cor de chá ou refrigerante de cola. Uma boa hidratação e evitar o uso de anti-inflamatórios são medidas importantes para a prevenção.

Maratona de Dublin bane corredor para sempre por uso de número alheio

Um corredor foi banido para o resto da vida da Maratona de Dublin por ter participado da prova usando um número de peito registrado em nome de uma mulher. Essa é uma prática que, infelizmente, vemos com frequência no Brasil, mas a punição rigorosa serve de exemplo. A organização da prova irlandesa mostrou que leva a sério a integridade da competição. Deveríamos imitar essa atitude por aqui para coibir esse tipo de fraude.

Mountain Do divulga calendário para 2027

O circuito Mountain Do, que tem parceria com o Corrida no Ar, já divulgou o seu calendário completo para 2027. A temporada começa em 14 de março com a etapa de Colonia del Sacramento, no Uruguai. Outras provas confirmadas incluem Praia do Rosa (SC), Deserto da Namíbia, Chapada dos Veadeiros (GO), Costão do Santinho (SC), Fim do Mundo (Argentina), Fernando de Noronha (PE), Selva Amazônica (AP), Deserto do Saara e Pantanal. Se você quer viver uma experiência de corrida incrível, as provas do Mountain Do são uma excelente pedida. Use o cupom CORRIDANOAR para ter 10% de desconto na sua inscrição. O link para o calendário completo está aqui.

Vega Sports troca Ticket Sports pela Sympla

No mundo dos negócios da corrida, uma mudança importante: a Vega Sports, organizadora de grandes provas como a Ayrton Senna Racing Day e a São Silvestre, está deixando a Ticket Sports e passando a usar a Sympla como sua plataforma de inscrições. A Vega provavelmente enfrentou dificuldades com a Ticket Sports em eventos passados e decidiu buscar um novo parceiro. Vamos ver como essa mudança impactará as próximas provas.

Desconto para o Uphill Cristo Redentor

A X3M, organizadora do circuito Uphill, está oferecendo um desconto de 30% para a etapa do Cristo Redentor. A prova, que acontece no dia 21 de novembro, tem largada às 17h30 e proporciona uma experiência única de subir o Corcovado correndo, terminando com a vista noturna do Rio de Janeiro aos pés do Cristo. Para aproveitar o desconto, use o cupom CORRIDANOAR30 ao se inscrever pelo link oficial. É uma oportunidade fantástica para quem busca um desafio inesquecível.
